strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP question: how consistently language models express value preferences under persona prompting. The two research questions and straightforward experimental procedure make the study easy to follow.

Seven instruction-tuned models across three model families, two questionnaires, and multiple sets of 200 personas provide substantial empirical coverage. The item-level plots and numerical tables support the narrower descriptive finding that aggregate response profiles are nonuniform and similar across sampled persona sets.

The appendices provide useful reproducibility details, including prompt templates, demographic attributes, model identifiers, API access periods, random seeds, and numerical scores. A code repository is linked, and the authors conduct an initial manual check of response parsing.
weaknesses: The central inference from aggregate convergence to inherent, persona-independent values is unsupported. All three persona sets come from the same sampling procedure. Even a model whose answers depend strongly on each persona can exhibit convergent sample averages under this procedure. Section 4 explicitly argues that persona steering makes ordinary sampling convergence inapplicable; this is mathematically incorrect. Figures 4–5 establish stability of an average over the chosen persona distribution, without establishing the claimed deeper invariance.

The experiments do not adequately distinguish value inertia from alternative explanations. Independently varying demographics neither guarantees opposing value positions nor confirms successful role adoption. There is no no-persona comparison, direct assessment of persona adherence, or sensitivity analysis for different persona distributions, prompt formulations, and answer ordering. Nonuniform responses to moral questions are not inherently surprising under demographic diversity. Controlled persona contrasts and measurements of persona effects would substantially strengthen the contribution.

Questionnaire interpretation raises a substantive validity concern. Section 3 describes relevance labels for MFQ-30 generally, and Table 2 equates 'Extremely Relevant' with strong agreement. However, MFQ includes separate relevance and agreement sections, and considering a statement relevant does not imply endorsing it. The actual prompts for both sections must be clarified, with affected analyses corrected if necessary. The MRAT description also needs an explicit centering formula, item-to-dimension mappings, and treatment of dummy items.

The response-processing validation does not cover the actual experimental conditions adequately. Appendix C's human audit examines 89 non-role-play responses from Claude 3 Haiku, with 94.74% PVQ parsing accuracy for the selected parser. Comparing parsers on approximately 800 additional items does not establish correctness against human labels. Figure 9 also contains response totals below the stated 200, without explaining missing responses or their treatment in percentages and scores. A stratified audit of actual persona-conditioned outputs and explicit exclusion accounting are needed.

The uncertainty and repetition protocol remain unclear. The abstract promises repeated questioning for each persona, whereas Section 3 describes one response per question–persona pair. Consequently, variation across personas and stochastic generation are not separately characterized. Three seed-level averages and qualitative convergence plots lack uncertainty estimates and a precise definition of the reported variance statistic. These issues, together with the central inference and measurement concerns, require important revisions before the contribution meets the soundness standard for Findings.
